title: Parenthood & the Parent Layer

myths.myth: Once kids arrive, the couple comes last.
myths.truth: Protecting your bond is good for the whole family.
myths.explanation: A strong partnership is the ground your kids grow on.

myths.myth: We'll just figure out the new load as we go.
myths.truth: Naming and sharing the load prevents resentment.
myths.explanation: Explicit fairness beats silent score-keeping under stress.

myths.myth: Intimacy should snap right back.
myths.truth: Rebuilding closeness takes time — and that's okay.
myths.explanation: Reconnecting at a healthy pace is normal after a baby.

myths.myth: Snapping at each other is just exhaustion.
myths.truth: Tired is real, but repair still matters.
myths.explanation: Sleep-deprivation explains a rupture; it doesn't excuse skipping the mend.

myths.myth: Fathers 'help out' with the kids.
myths.truth: Parenting is shared — a dad isn't a helper.
myths.explanation: Caregiving is a parent's job, not a favour.

myths.myth: Caring for babies just comes naturally to mums.
myths.truth: Hands-on parenting is learned by anyone.
myths.explanation: Skill, not gender, makes a confident caregiver.

myths.myth: The mental load of parenting is hers to carry.
myths.truth: Tracking appointments and needs should be shared.
myths.explanation: The invisible planning work belongs to both parents.

myths.myth: Kids don't notice who does what.
myths.truth: Children learn equality by watching their parents.
myths.explanation: Modelling a fair home shapes how kids see gender.

myths.myth: Good parents put themselves last, always.
myths.truth: Looking after yourself lets you look after them.
myths.explanation: Your needs matter too — depletion helps no one.

myths.myth: Postpartum sadness is just being dramatic.
myths.truth: Postpartum depression is real and treatable.
myths.explanation: It deserves support and care, not dismissal.

myths.myth: Dads don't get postpartum struggles.
myths.truth: New fathers can struggle too — and deserve support.
myths.explanation: Parental mental health isn't only a mother's issue.

myths.myth: Burnout means I'm a bad parent.
myths.truth: Burnout is a sign to get support, not a verdict.
myths.explanation: Running on empty is a signal, not a failing.

myths.myth: Talking about bodies will put ideas in their head.
myths.truth: Honest, age-right answers keep kids safer.
myths.explanation: Knowing the real words and boundaries protects children.

myths.myth: 'The talk' is one big conversation.
myths.truth: It's many small talks over the years.
myths.explanation: Age-by-age conversations beat one awkward lecture.

myths.myth: If I don't know the answer, I should make one up.
myths.truth: 'Let's find out together' is a great answer.
myths.explanation: Honesty keeps the door open for the next question.

myths.myth: Schools can handle all of it.
myths.truth: Your facts plus your values are what they remember.
myths.explanation: Parents add the values that anchor the facts.

myths.myth: A slap never hurt anyone.
myths.truth: Hitting teaches fear, not better behaviour.
myths.explanation: Positive, firm, kind discipline works without harm.

myths.myth: Fear is the same as respect.
myths.truth: Respect grows from warmth and firm limits, not fear.
myths.explanation: Children follow boundaries best when they feel safe.

myths.myth: I turned out fine, so it must be fine.
myths.truth: You can keep the love and drop the harm you inherited.
myths.explanation: Breaking the cycle means choosing which patterns to pass on.

myths.myth: Losing my temper means I've ruined it.
myths.truth: Repair after a rupture is what kids remember.
myths.explanation: A calm 'I'm sorry, let's try again' rebuilds trust.

myths.myth: It's just a phase you can talk them out of.
myths.truth: Affirming your child keeps them safe and well.
myths.explanation: Acceptance protects mental health; pressure harms it.

myths.myth: Strict gender rules will set them straight.
myths.truth: Forcing norms harms; following the child helps.
myths.explanation: Don't force a box — let the child lead, with no pressure to label.

myths.myth: A coming-out is something to fix.
myths.truth: Meet it with love — be their safe place.
myths.explanation: Respond to questioning or coming-out with affirmation.

myths.myth: Talking about identity will 'make' them LGBTQ+.
myths.truth: Acceptance doesn't cause identity; it protects kids.
myths.explanation: Openness keeps a child safe; it doesn't shape who they are.

myths.myth: A struggling child just needs stricter parenting.
myths.truth: Neurodivergence isn't bad parenting or naughtiness.
myths.explanation: Autism, ADHD and learning differences aren't a discipline problem.

myths.myth: They'll simply grow out of it.
myths.truth: The right support and accommodations help them thrive.
myths.explanation: Adjusting home and school is what helps, not waiting.

myths.myth: A diagnosis is just a label.
myths.truth: Understanding their profile is how you advocate for them.
myths.explanation: Knowing their needs unlocks the right support.

myths.myth: It's something to feel ashamed of.
myths.truth: It's no one's fault — and nothing to hide.
myths.explanation: Dropping the shame helps the whole family.

myths.myth: Cracking down hard will fix it.
myths.truth: Calm, connected responses work better than rupture.
myths.explanation: Respond, don't rupture — connection keeps them reachable.

myths.myth: It's just a lack of willpower.
myths.truth: Dependence is a health issue, not a character flaw.
myths.explanation: Substance, screen and gaming dependence need help, not blame.

myths.myth: Good kids don't get addicted.
myths.truth: It can happen in any family — early help matters.
myths.explanation: Getting help early beats waiting for it to pass.

myths.myth: Bringing it up will only push them away.
myths.truth: Staying connected is what keeps the door open.
myths.explanation: Calm, shame-free conversation keeps the relationship intact.

myths.myth: Abuse is mostly strangers.
myths.truth: Most harm comes from someone known — stay alert and open.
myths.explanation: Being the trusted, watchful adult is the best protection.

myths.myth: A child who tells might be making it up.
myths.truth: Believe first — children rarely invent abuse.
myths.explanation: Responding to a disclosure starts with believing.

myths.myth: Body-safety talks will scare them.
myths.truth: Body-safety talks make kids safer, not fearful.
myths.explanation: Knowing names, boundaries and who to tell keeps children safe.

myths.myth: A disclosure is somehow the child's fault.
myths.truth: The child is always the protected victim — never to blame.
myths.explanation: Under POCSO, the child is the protected party, full stop.

capstone.name: Raising the Next Generation
capstone.landing: The loop comes full circle: the parent-layer tools — equal parenting, self-care, the age-by-age talks, breaking the cycle, safeguarding — earned across Chapter 8, inherited harms erased as faint ghosts under the truths, Sam handing the eraser and pencil to the next generation.

canvasFeel: Adult / dark theme on the dotted-paper texture — warm parent-layer motifs (a pram, a shared chore wheel, a broken-cycle arrow, a safe-adult shield) glowing on deep violet night paper; struck-through inherited myths ('a slap never hurt me', 'fathers help') rubbed out by UN, positive-parenting truths written by RE.
